objectives: To carry out the experiment as outlined in the laboratory manual.
apparatus: Mild steel plane (adjustable angle), slider trays with different liners, cord, pulley at the end of the plane, hanger and slotted masses, ball-bearing tray (three wheels), laboratory scale, protractor or angle scale, and a ruler.

theory.text:
Friction is the force that resists motion between two surfaces in contact. It acts along the surfaces, opposite to the direction of motion. Its size is given by

F = μN

where μ is the coefficient of friction (it has no units and depends on the two surfaces) and N is the normal reaction. Friction does not depend on the area of contact.

Level plane (Part A1): When the tray moves at a slow, constant velocity, it is not accelerating, so the net force is zero. The pulling force P equals the friction force, and the normal reaction equals the weight, N = W. So P = μW, which gives μ = P/W. A graph of P against W is a straight line whose slope is μ.

Angle of friction (Part A2): On a tilted plane, the weight has two components: W sin θ along the plane (trying to slide the tray down) and W cos θ into the plane (the normal reaction). At the critical angle the tray just starts to slide, so W sin θ = μW cos θ. This gives tan θ = μ, and θ is called the angle of friction (or angle of repose).

Inclined plane (Part B): The tray is pulled parallel to the plane at constant velocity.

Up the plane, friction and W sin θ both act down the slope, so P = W(sin θ + μ cos θ).

Down the plane, friction acts up the slope and W sin θ helps the motion, so P = W(μ cos θ − sin θ).

Rolling friction: With ball-bearing wheels, sliding is replaced by rolling, which has much less resistance. With no friction the force needed would be P = W sin θ. The actual force is P_A = P + F, where F is the rolling resistance, so F = P_A − W sin θ.

precautions: The friction force increased as the load increased.
The force needed to pull the tray up the plane was larger than the force needed to pull it down.
The ball-bearing tray needed much less force than the sliding trays.
Different liner materials gave different values of μ.
The plane was levelled before Part A.
The tray was moved at a slow, constant velocity, not accelerated.
The cord was kept parallel to the plane.
Readings were taken at eye level to avoid parallax error.
The trays and masses were weighed on the scale, and the plane was kept clean and dry.
content.discussion:
Sources of error
It is hard to tell when the tray is moving at exactly constant velocity, so the added mass is slightly off.
Friction in the pulley and stiffness of the cord.
Parallax when reading the protractor, so θ is only accurate to about ±[ ]°.
Dust or uneven surfaces changed μ from one run to another. This is why the manual says to expect some scatter.
The cord may not have been perfectly parallel to the plane.

learnings: Applied theoretical principles to experimental measurement.
